claims.text: Chromium-based electroplating of stainless steel will improve its corrosion resistance in challenging environments.
The initial material is annealed austenitic SS304 stainless steel.
The chromium-based coating is 10 microns thick.
The coating is electroplated at a current density of 10 mA/cm^2 for 2 hours.
Chromium electroplating produces a chromium oxide layer on the SS304 surface.
The chromium oxide layer acts as a barrier to corrosive species.
The chromium oxide layer reduces the diffusion of ions through the surface.
Reduced ion diffusion enhances the corrosion resistance of the coated SS304.
The coated SS304 will exhibit a 30% lower corrosion rate than uncoated SS304 in the same environment.
The coated SS304 corrosion rate will be below 0.1 mm/year.
The magnitude of the corrosion-resistance improvement depends on coating parameters and environmental conditions.

contradictions.description: The predicted outcome specifies a 30% corrosion-rate reduction, but the falsification rule accepts any reduction of at least 20%; therefore, a 20–29% reduction would fail to meet the stated prediction while not falsifying it.

The boundary requires a corrosion rate below 0.1 mm/year, whereas the falsification rule uses only a relative 20% reduction. Depending on the baseline rate, the experiment could pass the relative criterion while violating the absolute boundary.
